GrantedAccess: 0x1010

triage.summary: User CORP\it.helpdesk remotely logged into domain controller DC-02.corp.local from 10.20.4.77 and ran an unsigned svchost.exe from C:\Users\Public\Libraries that accessed lsass.exe, consistent with credential dumping.
triage.severity_reason: Credential dumping from LSASS on a domain controller by a remote user indicates likely domain compromise.
behaviors: remotely logging in to a domain controller with an unusual logon type
executing an unsigned masquerading process from a public user directory
accessing the LSASS process to read credentials
gaining special privileges on the domain controller

techniques.name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
techniques.description: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct Lateral Movement using Use Alternate Authentication Material. As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system.

detections.name: Detection of Credential Dumping from LSASS Memory via Access and Dump Sequence

analytics.description: A non-privileged or abnormal process attempts to open a handle with full access (0x1F0FFF) to lsass.exe and subsequently invokes memory dump, file creation, or registry modification indicative of credential scraping. This behavior chain reflects staged credential theft activity.

techniques.name: Modify Authentication Process: Domain Controller Authentication
techniques.description: Adversaries may patch the authentication process on a domain controller to bypass the typical authentication mechanisms and enable access to accounts. Malware may be used to inject false credentials into the authentication process on a domain controller with the intent of creating a backdoor used to access any user’s account and/or credentials (ex: Skeleton Key). Skeleton key works through a patch on an enterprise domain controller authentication process (LSASS) with credentials that adversaries may use to bypass the standard authentication system. Once patched, an adversary can use the injected password to successfully authenticate as any domain user account (until the the skeleton key is erased from memory by a reboot of the domain controller). Authenticated access may enable unfettered access to hosts and/or resources within single-factor authentication environments.

playbook.title: Credential Dumping via Unauthorized svchost on DC-02
playbook.executive_summary: A remote interactive RDP logon (Logon Type 10) by CORP\it.helpdesk from 10.20.4.77 launched an unsigned svchost.exe that accessed LSASS on DC-02.corp.local, indicating credential dumping (T1003.001). Immediate containment, evidence collection, eradication, recovery, and hardening are required to protect the domain.

detection_and_analysis.action: Collect volatile memory and process state from DC-02.corp.local
detection_and_analysis.detail: Acquire a RAM image and list of running processes, focusing on svchost.exe and LSASS handles, using a trusted forensic tool.

detection_and_analysis.action: Correlate Sysmon EventID 10 with Security EventIDs 4624 and 4672
detection_and_analysis.detail: Search WinEventLog:Security and WinEventLog:Sysmon for the timestamps of the remote RDP logon and LSASS access to confirm scope and identify related events.

detection_and_analysis.action: Identify additional hosts using the same credentials
detection_and_analysis.detail: Query domain controller logs for other Logon Type 10 events by CORP\it.helpdesk around the same time across the network.

containment.detail: Place the server in a quarantine VLAN and disable remote RDP to stop further credential exfiltration.
Use taskkill or PowerShell to stop C:\Users\Public\Libraries\svchost.exe and revoke its token.
Lock the account in Active Directory and reset its password to prevent reuse.

eradication.detail: Delete C:\Users\Public\Libraries\svchost.exe and any related artifacts; verify file hash is no longer present.

eradication.action: Scan DC-02 for additional malicious modules
eradication.detail: Run a full anti‑malware scan and verify no other unauthorized binaries are present.

eradication.action: Reset LSASS security descriptors to default
eradication.detail: Reapply default permissions so only SYSTEM and authorized services can access LSASS.

recovery.action: Restore DC-02 from a known‑good backup or rebuild from a clean image
recovery.detail: If integrity cannot be assured, reinstall the OS, apply latest patches, and re‑join it to the domain.

recovery.action: Re‑enable the CORP\it.helpdesk account with MFA
recovery.detail: After investigation, reactivate the account and enforce multi‑factor authentication.

recovery.action: Enable continuous monitoring for LSASS access attempts
recovery.detail: Deploy real‑time alerts for Sysmon EventID 10 targeting LSASS on all domain controllers.

hardening.action: Enforce privileged process integrity for LSASS
hardening.detail: Configure Windows Defender Application Control or similar to block unsigned binaries from accessing LSASS.
Require Just‑In‑Time elevation and limit remote interactive logons for high‑privilege accounts.
Enable Credential Guard and restrict remote interactive logons to approved admin workstations.

hunt_leads.look_for: Additional Logon Type 10 events by CORP\it.helpdesk or other privileged accounts outside business hours
ProcessAccess events where GrantedAccess includes 0x1010 to lsass.exe from non‑system binaries
Repeated credential‑dumping patterns such as consecutive LSASS handle opens from the same source host

issues: Mapped technique T1556.001 (Modify Authentication Process: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay) is not supported by the alert. The alert shows a legitimate RDP logon (Logon Type 10) followed by LSASS access — there is no evidence of name-service poisoning or SMB relay. Remove T1556.001 from the mapped techniques.

The containment step 'Terminate the malicious svchost.exe process' (taskkill/PowerShell) destroys volatile evidence (process memory, handles) before it is collected. The detection phase only says to 'collect volatile memory and process state' but does not guarantee it is completed before termination. The playbook should explicitly require that a full memory capture and process handle dump be completed and verified before the process is terminated, or the termination step should be removed/推迟
